name: skani
desc: Fast, robust ANI and aligned fraction for (metagenomic) genomes and contigs
why: Fast average nucleotide identity estimation for metagenomic genomes is real bioinformatics you can run on your own sequences.

brief.what_it_is: skani is a command-line program that calculates average nucleotide identity (ANI) and aligned fraction (AF) between DNA sequences such as genomes, MAGs (metagenome-assembled genomes), and contigs, for ANI above roughly 80%. You give it FASTA files, and it prints tab-separated results with the ANI and the fraction of each genome aligned. It has three main modes: pairwise or all-vs-all comparison (dist), searching a query against a prebuilt sketch database (search), and building a similarity matrix or edge list for a folder of genomes (triangle). The README describes it as an approximate mapping method that avoids base-level alignment, combined with a k-mer sketching filter.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says skani is meant for large-scale microbial genomics and for comparing incomplete MAGs, where it claims to be more accurate than pure sketching methods such as Mash, which 'may underestimate ANI for incomplete MAGs'. It is also aimed at speed on huge, diverse datasets.
brief.how_it_works: skani uses an approximate mapping method without base-level alignment to estimate ANI, and a fast k-mer sketching filter to make comparisons across very large collections feasible. Sketches can be saved to a database with skani sketch and searched later with skani search. The README does not go into further internal detail; the Nature Methods paper it cites describes sparse chaining.

commands_seen.context: Installs the released skani package from the bioconda channel (Option 1 in the README).
Builds and installs skani from a cloned source directory using the Rust toolchain; the README says the default install location is ~/.cargo.
Quick start: computes ANI and aligned fraction for two genomes; the README notes skani is symmetric, so argument order does not change ANI.

commands_seen.cmd: skani dist -t 3 -q query1.fa query2.fa -r reference1.fa reference2.fa -o all-to-all_results.txt
commands_seen.context: Compares multiple query and reference genomes using 3 threads and writes results to a file.
Compares individual FASTA records (for example contigs) inside the query and reference files rather than whole files.
Builds a reusable sketch database from a set of genomes for memory-efficient searching.
Searches one or more query genomes against a previously built sketch database.
Writes an all-vs-all ANI similarity matrix for all genomes in a folder.
Same all-vs-all comparison but written as an edge list (-E).
Downloads the prebuilt statically compiled executable for x86-64 Linux (Option 3); followed by chmod +x skani and ./skani -h.

brief.install_notes: Three options: conda via bioconda; building from source, which needs Rust with cargo in PATH, a C compiler such as GCC, and make, and takes a few minutes depending on core count; or a prebuilt static binary for x86-64 Linux only. The README says the static binary runs about 3-10% slower most of the time and can be drastically slower on some tasks. No accounts, API keys, or config files are mentioned. For searching, you either download a pre-sketched database from the wiki or build one yourself with skani sketch; the README cites about 6 GB RAM for searching a database of more than 65,000 prokaryotic genomes. The clustering script in scripts/ needs python3, seaborn, scipy/numpy, and matplotlib.
brief.standout: It reports aligned fraction alongside ANI, so you can tell how much of each genome the ANI is based on, which matters for incomplete MAGs. The README claims it is about 40-50x faster than FastANI and nearly as fast as Mash on very diverse datasets, while avoiding Mash's underestimation on incomplete MAGs.
brief.status: Maintained, per the README. It names a single active developer (Jim Shaw), announces v0.4.0 as released with a dated note of October 2026, and links a CHANGELOG. I could not see commit history or release dates on the page itself, so this rests on the README's own statements.
brief.caveats: Output is suppressed when aligned fraction is below 15%, so with default parameters only results above roughly 82% ANI are reliably reported; lower-ANI comparisons need advanced options. Result order is not guaranteed to be deterministic with more than 5000 query genomes. v0.4.0 changed the sketch format as a breaking change: v0.3.x and earlier cannot read v0.4 sketches, and v0.4 works with old databases but is slower on them until converted. The prebuilt binary is Linux x86-64 only and can be slower. The Rust API has no stability guarantee and minimal docs. The Python bindings (pyskani) are by a different author, and the README disclaims their correctness. The README does not state a license in the text I read.
quotes: skani is accurate for isolate genomes and incomplete metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Pure sketching methods (e.g. Mash) may underestimate ANI for incomplete MAGs.
skani can search a genome against a preprocessed database of >65000 prokaryotic genomes in seconds (~6 GB RAM) by using a fast k-mer filter.
In practice, this means that only results with > ~82% ANI are reliably output (with default parameters).
fetch_log: https://github.com/bluenote-1577/skani: fetched OK, README returned in full. Did not follow further links; the README was complete enough to write the brief from.

judge.reason: skani makes genome relatedness practical at scale, and pairing ANI with aligned fraction reveals when incomplete genomes make a similarity score misleading.

entry.title: skani
entry.tldr: Compares two DNA genomes and prints how similar they are and how much of each lines up, fast enough to search tens of thousands of genomes in seconds.
entry.deeper_look:
skani calculates average nucleotide identity (ANI) and aligned fraction (AF) between genomes, metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and contigs. You hand it FASTA files and it prints a tab-separated table: the ANI, and how much of each genome the comparison actually covered. It works for sequences above roughly 80% ANI.

It has three main modes. `dist` compares genomes pairwise or all-vs-all. `search` looks up query genomes in a prebuilt sketch database. `triangle` takes a folder of genomes and writes a similarity matrix or an edge list. Sketches are built once with `skani sketch` and reused.

The idea underneath is a trade between exact alignment and cheap sketching. Pure k-mer sketching tools such as Mash are fast but, per the README, "may underestimate ANI for incomplete MAGs". skani uses approximate mapping with no base-level alignment, plus a k-mer sketch filter to skip hopeless pairs. The cited Nature Methods paper describes the method as sparse chaining. Reporting aligned fraction next to ANI tells you whether a high identity rests on the whole genome or only a small piece.

That makes it a way into microbial genomics: how species are drawn by sequence similarity, why incomplete assemblies complicate that, and how comparison scales to databases of tens of thousands of genomes.
entry.install:
brew install skani
# Needs your own FASTA genome files. Alternatives: conda install -c bioconda skani, or build from source with Rust.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the subcommands (dist, sketch, search, triangle) and their options.
Prints ANI and aligned fraction for the two genomes. Argument order does not change the ANI.
Compares every genome in the folder against every other and writes an all-vs-all ANI matrix.

entry.whats_unique: It reports aligned fraction alongside ANI, so you can see how much of each genome the number is based on. The README claims it is about 40-50x faster than FastANI and close to Mash's speed on very diverse datasets.
entry.caveats: With default parameters only results above roughly 82% ANI are reliably reported, and v0.4 changed the sketch format in a breaking way, so older sketches are not readable by v0.3.x and earlier.
